opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because the way I see it, we've spent decades forcing everything onto one substrate: deterministic digital logic. That made sense historically, but it doesn't match the structure of the problems we actually care about.

I'd break it into three regimes.

**Deterministic computers** are still the backbone for anything that needs exactness and reliability: control flow, bookkeeping, databases, compilers, cryptography, the orchestration layer that ties everything together. When you need the same answer every time, bit-for-bit, you use deterministic logic. That's not going away.

**Probabilistic computers** are where I think a huge amount of AI workloads naturally belong. If you look at what modern machine learning actually does, it's mostly sampling, inference, and reasoning under uncertainty. Generative models are fundamentally about learning distributions and drawing samples from them. On a deterministic chip, you're spending enormous energy to suppress noise, guaranteeing every bit is exactly a zero or a one, and then you burn more compute generating pseudo-randomness to simulate stochasticity on top. That's backwards. Physics is already noisy and thermal. If you build hardware that harnesses that noise as a computational resource, you can sample from complex distributions far more efficiently. So I'd put the bulk of generative modeling, Bayesian inference, energy-based models, and Monte Carlo-style workloads there over time.

**Quantum computers** are for a narrower but very deep slice: problems where the underlying structure is quantum mechanical. Simulating molecules, materials, chemistry, quantum field theories, certain kinds of quantum data. Classical simulation of those systems scales exponentially in the worst case, so quantum hardware is the natural fit. I'm skeptical of claims that quantum will accelerate everything; it's not a general-purpose replacement. It's a specialized co-processor for nature's quantum parts.

So the picture I have in mind is heterogeneous: a deterministic host orchestrating, probabilistic accelerators doing most of the inference and generative heavy lifting, and quantum co-processors called for the inherently quantum subroutines. The deeper principle is matching the physics of the hardware to the structure of the computation. Whenever you have a mismatch, you pay for it in energy and time, and at the scale AI is heading, that cost becomes the bottleneck. Getting this division right is, in my view, one of the main levers for scaling intelligence per watt.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that there's a natural hierarchy of computational substrates, and each one is really matched to a different class of problems based on the physics of the problem itself.

Deterministic computing, your classical CPUs and GPUs, is for everything where you need exact, reproducible answers: arithmetic, control logic, memory, the traditional workloads. That's not going away. It's the backbone, and it's absurdly cheap per operation at this point.

But a huge fraction of what we actually want machines to do now is probabilistic in nature. Inference, sampling, generative models, Bayesian reasoning, optimization under uncertainty. Right now we simulate randomness on deterministic hardware, which is kind of silly. You're spending enormous amounts of energy to pretend your transistors are noisy, when physics will happily give you noise for free. Thermodynamic or stochastic computing is about embracing that: you build hardware where the natural fluctuations of the system are the computational resource. You let the device relax to an equilibrium distribution and sample from it directly. For things like Langevin dynamics, diffusion models, Gaussian process inference, linear algebra with uncertainty, that can be orders of magnitude more efficient than a GPU doing Monte Carlo.

And then quantum is the narrowest tier. Quantum computers are specialized for problems where the underlying structure is genuinely quantum: simulating molecules, materials, certain cryptographic and algebraic problems, maybe some optimization with specific structure. People get excited and think quantum will eat machine learning, but most machine learning workloads don't have the interference structure that quantum advantage requires, and the overhead of error correction is brutal. So you reserve it for cases where nature is quantum and you're trying to model nature.

The way I'd summarize it: if the problem is logical, use deterministic hardware. If the problem is statistical, use probabilistic hardware. If the problem is quantum mechanical, use quantum hardware. Match the physics of the computer to the physics of the question. And in practice these will be heterogeneous systems, with a classical controller orchestrating thermodynamic accelerators and, eventually, quantum coprocessors for the rare workloads that truly need them.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful way to divide them is by what structure the workload has. If you need precise arithmetic, reliable control flow, or to move data around, deterministic computers are very good at that. There’s no reason to give that up.

If the problem is inherently about uncertainty—sampling from a distribution, exploring possible solutions, doing inference—then a probabilistic computer can be a natural fit. Instead of treating randomness as something you have to simulate, you make it part of the computational machinery. But you still have to ask whether it produces useful samples efficiently.

Quantum computers give you a different set of resources: superposition, entanglement, and interference. They’re particularly interesting for problems with quantum structure, like simulating quantum systems. They aren’t simply faster probabilistic computers, and you shouldn’t expect them to accelerate every optimization or machine-learning workload.

So I’d picture a heterogeneous system. A deterministic computer orchestrates the computation, and you send particular subproblems to probabilistic or quantum hardware where there’s a demonstrated advantage. The practical question is whether that advantage survives the costs of encoding the problem, transferring data, and reading the result. You want to accelerate the whole workflow, not just an isolated mathematical step.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to look at the structure of the problem and ask which substrate can do the relevant computation most efficiently. Deterministic computers are very good at precise logic, arithmetic, and coordinating a workflow. If you need an exact, reproducible answer, that’s generally where you want to be.

Probabilistic computers become interesting when sampling is the workload. In machine learning, for example, you’re often trying to represent a distribution, explore possible configurations, or estimate an expectation. Instead of spending a lot of deterministic computation generating randomness and manipulating samples, you can potentially use hardware whose dynamics do some of that work directly.

Quantum computers offer a different resource: interference and entanglement. They’re particularly compelling for simulating quantum systems, where representing the state on a classical machine can become extremely expensive. But being quantum doesn’t automatically make a device a better sampler or a faster optimizer for every problem. You need an algorithm that actually exploits those resources, and you have to account for the cost of getting data in and results out.

So I’d expect heterogeneous systems. A deterministic machine orchestrates the computation, a probabilistic processor handles suitable sampling tasks, and a quantum processor handles particular subproblems where there’s a demonstrated advantage. The division should follow the total cost of solving the problem—including communication, precision, and error correction—rather than a preference for one kind of computer.
